# Time series analysis {#sec-time-series}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

library(rebook)
chapterPreamble(cache = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: options
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    message = FALSE,
    fig.width = 10,
    dpi = 300,
    dev = "png",
    dev.args = list(type = "cairo-png")
)
```

Microbial communities are dynamic, constantly evolving over time. However,
despite temporal fluctuations driven by environmental and other factors, the
microbiome retains its core characteristics [@Schmidt2018].

Cross-sectional studies capture the microbiome at a single time point. In
contrast, longitudinal (temporal) study designs follow the same individuals
over time. This allows researchers to study how microbial communities change,
for example, in response to an intervention such as antibiotic or probiotic
treatment, or during the progression of a disease.

Longitudinal data also help to interpret cross-sectional findings. A single
sample reflects not only differences between individuals but also the natural
day-to-day variability within each individual's microbiome. By sampling the
same subjects repeatedly, this within-subject variability can be estimated and
separated from between-subject differences. This reduces the uncertainty in
comparisons between groups.

Repeated sampling also reveals the dynamics of a community, such as whether
a taxon has alternative stable states with a tipping point between them
(@fig-ts-stability). Such dynamics can be reconstructed from one long time
series, but many short time series from different subjects can be even more
informative [@Ross2026].

![Stability landscape of a bistable taxon. (a, b) The abundance has two
stable states (blue and red) separated by a tipping point (orange); the
landscape has deterministic and stochastic components. (c, d) The same
dynamics can be observed in one long time series or in many short time
series from different subjects. (e) Short time series from many subjects
recover the true stationary density faster. Reproduced from @Ross2026 under
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](figures/time_series_stability.png){#fig-ts-stability
fig-alt="Panels showing a double-well stability landscape with two stable
states and a tipping point, its drift and diffusion functions, one long
time series switching between two states, many short time series from
several subjects, and a plot where multiple short time series reach
agreement with the true density sooner than one long series."}

Analyzing longitudinal data includes aspects that need to be taken into
account, such as the dependence between samples collected from the same
subject.

Most of the methods introduced in
[OMA](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/) can be applied to longitudinal data
with small modifications. This chapter shows how alpha diversity, beta
diversity and differential abundance analyses can be applied to longitudinal
data. The difference is that samples from the same subject are paired, and the
analysis has to take this into account. For further methods, see the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("miaTime")` package.

In this chapter, we use the peerj32 data set
([OMA data sets](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/docs/devel/pages/data_sets.html#sec-data-peerj32))
from a
probiotic/placebo intervention study. It includes gut microbiota samples from
22 subjects at 2 time points. The first time point was sampled before
introducing a treatment.

```{r}
#| label: load_data

library(mia)
library(microbiomeDataSets)

mae <- peerj32()
tse <- getWithColData(mae, 1L)
tse[["time_point"]] <- tse[["time"]] |> as.factor()
```

## Alpha diversity

[OMA](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/docs/devel/pages/alpha_diversity.html) introduces alpha diversity. Here we calculate the
Shannon index and visualize it by time point (@fig-time-alpha-shannon). Lines
connect the samples of each subject.

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-alpha-shannon
#| fig-cap: "Shannon diversity in the peerj32 data at the two time points, faceted and coloured by intervention group (LGG and placebo). Lines connect the samples of the same subject."

library(miaViz)

tse <- addAlpha(tse, index = "shannon")

plotBoxplot(
    tse,
    col.var = "shannon",
    x = "time_point",
    pair.by = "subject",
    colour.by = "group",
    facet.by = "group"
)
```

The plot does not show a clear change in either group. Because the samples are
paired, we use the paired Wilcoxon test separately for each group.

```{r}
#| label: alpha_wilcoxon

df <- colData(tse) |> as.data.frame()
df <- df[order(df[["subject"]]), ]

lapply(split(df, df[["group"]]), function(x) {
    wilcox.test(
        x[x[["time_point"]] == 1, "shannon"],
        x[x[["time_point"]] == 2, "shannon"],
        paired = TRUE
    )
})
```

Neither group shows a significant change in Shannon diversity between the
time points. The tests above do not compare the groups. A linear mixed model
can test whether the change over time differs between the groups. The
`time * group` term includes the effects of time and group and their
interaction, and `(1 | subject)` adds a random effect for each subject to
account for the repeated measurements.

```{r}
#| label: alpha_lmm

library(lmerTest)

model <- lmer(shannon ~ time * group + (1 | subject), data = df)
summary(model)
```

The interaction term "time:groupPlacebo" tests whether the change in Shannon
diversity from the first to the second time point differs between the Placebo
and LGG groups. The interaction is not significant, so the change in diversity
does not differ between the groups.

## Beta diversity

[OMA](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/docs/devel/pages/community_similarity.html) introduces ordination. In longitudinal data, we
can connect the samples of each subject in the ordination plot to show how the
communities changed over time (@fig-time-beta-ordination).

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-beta-ordination
#| fig-cap: "MDS ordination of the peerj32 samples based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity of relative abundances, coloured by intervention group. Arrows connect the samples of each subject from the first to the second time point."

tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")
tse <- addMDS(tse, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray")

plotOrdination(
    tse,
    dimred = "MDS",
    colour.by = "group",
    pair.by = "subject",
    sort.by = "time"
)
```

The arrows show no consistent shift that would separate the groups.

The change can also be quantified as the dissimilarity between consecutive
samples of the same subject, i.e., divergence (see [OMA](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/docs/devel/pages/community_similarity.html#sec-divergence)).
@fig-time-divergence shows the divergence by intervention group.

```{r}
#| label: fig-time-divergence
#| fig-cap: "Bray-Curtis divergence between consecutive samples of the same subject in the peerj32 data, shown by intervention group (LGG and placebo)."

library(miaTime)

tse <- addStepwiseDivergence(
    tse,
    time.col = "time",
    group = "subject",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray"
)

plotBoxplot(
    tse,
    col.var = "divergence",
    x = "group"
)
```

Divergence between the time points is similar in both groups.

## Differential abundance

[OMA](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/docs/devel/pages/differential_abundance.html) introduces differential abundance analysis. With
paired samples, the subject has to be included in the model. Below, we use
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("LimROTS")` [@Anwar2025] to test which taxa changed
between the time points in the LGG group. The argument `correlation_block`
specifies the subject, so that samples from the same subject are resampled
together and their correlation is accounted for in the model. LimROTS requires
log-transformed data, so we use the robust CLR (rclr) transformation.

```{r}
#| label: daa_limrots

library(LimROTS)

tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "rclr")
tse_lgg <- tse[, tse[["group"]] == "LGG"]

set.seed(123)
tse_lgg <- LimROTS(
    tse_lgg,
    assay.type = "rclr",
    niter = 200,
    meta.info = c("time_point", "subject"),
    group = "time_point",
    formula.str = "~ 0 + time_point",
    correlation_block = "subject",
    verbose = FALSE
)

res <- rowData(tse_lgg)[, c("corrected.logfc", "pvalue", "qvalue")]
# Sort the results
res <- res[order(res[["pvalue"]]), ]
res |> head()
```

`corrected.logfc` is the first time point minus the second, so negative values
mean higher abundance at the second time point. In the LGG group,
*`r rownames(res)[[1L]]`*
`r ifelse(res[1, "corrected.logfc"] > 0, "decreased", "increased")` after the
intervention. However, the result is not significant which we can see from
adjusted p-values (qvalue).

LimROTS compares the levels of one categorical variable. To test whether the
change differs between the groups, use a model with an interaction term as in
the alpha diversity example above.
